Hello, Dr. Lee. I... well, I'm here because things at work have gotten completely out of hand with the whispering and the talking. I'm the chief executive of my company, so, you know, I expect a certain level of office politics and chatter, but this is... it's beyond that now. I keep hearing people talking about me. It’s usually the board members, or sometimes my senior staff, and they’re just constantly saying that I’m ruining the company, that I'm destroying everything we've built and driving our margins into the ground. 

But the strange thing is where I'm hearing it from. I'll be in my private office, and I can hear them plotting and talking about me right through the conference room walls. And our walls are supposed to be thick, soundproofed architectural glass, but I hear them clear as day. And if it's not the walls, it's my phone. I'll have my phone sitting on the desk, completely powered off—screen black, completely shut down so I can try to get some peace and quiet to review contracts—and I can still hear their voices coming right out of the device, criticizing my decisions and saying I'm a failure. 

It sounds so incredibly real, so loud and clear, that I actually answer them. I'll just start defending myself, talking right back to the wall or yelling at the dead phone, explaining my strategy and telling them they don't know what they're talking about... and I'll be halfway through a sentence before I look up and see my assistant staring at me from the doorway, and I realize... I realize no one else heard them. No one else heard a single word. But they're so loud, Doctor. I just don't understand how no one else is hearing them when they are right there.
Can you tell me how long you've been hearing these voices — when did this first start?

Well, let me think back... it's been about three months. Yes, I'd say exactly three months, because I remember precisely what I was working on when it first started. We were in the middle of our quarterly review, which is always a high-stress period, obviously, and I was going over the profit margins for our new product line. I had shut my phone completely off—powered down, black screen, just like I was saying before—because I needed absolute, total concentration. 

And that was the very first time I heard them. It was the CFO and one of our lead investors, and their voices were coming right out of that dead phone. That was three months ago. At first, I tried to rationalize it, you know? I thought maybe it was some bizarre Bluetooth glitch, or maybe the phone wasn't actually off and a conference call had auto-connected somehow. I even had my IT department run a full sweep of my devices because I thought maybe we were being hacked, or maybe there was some kind of frequency interference in the building's wiring. I made them check everything. But they didn't find a single thing, and the voices just kept going. 

So it's been a solid three months of this. Three months of hearing them through the phone, and then it started coming through the architectural glass walls shortly after that. Ninety days of just... constant, relentless criticism while I'm trying to do my job. You have no idea how exhausting it is to have to argue with a wall for three months straight just to defend your own business strategy, especially when you're the one who built the company from the ground up.

Over these past three months, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low, or on the other end, unusually energetic, elated, or needing much less sleep than normal?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm stressed, obviously. Anyone would be stressed if they had to deal with what I'm dealing with. But as far as being depressed or hopeless? Absolutely not. I'm not sitting around crying or feeling sorry for myself. I have a company to run. I have hundreds of employees relying on me to make payroll and secure contracts and keep the lights on, so I don't have the luxury of just... giving up and feeling low. I'm actually incredibly driven right now, probably more driven than I've been in years, because I have to prove them wrong. Every time I hear them through the wall saying I'm ruining the margins, it just makes me want to work harder to show them the quarterly projections are solid. 

And as for the other thing, being unusually energetic or elated? No, I wouldn't say that either. I'm not bouncing off the walls or feeling euphoric or anything like that. I'm just... focused. Hyper-focused, maybe, because of the constant scrutiny. I'm sleeping about the same as I always do. Well, maybe a little less, but that's just because I'm a CEO, and sleep is a commodity I don't always have time for. I might get four or five hours a night, but that's been my baseline for the last decade. It's not some sudden change where I feel like I don't need sleep at all. I definitely feel tired when I wake up, but I push through it with coffee and sheer willpower, just like I always have. 

So, no, my mood is fine. My energy levels are normal for someone in my position. It's just the voices. If I could just get them to stop talking about me through the phone and the glass, everything else would be perfectly fine. I just need to figure out how they're doing it so I can put a stop to it and get back to managing my company in peace.
Have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements—especially anything like stimulants—around the time these voices started or since?

No, absolutely not. I mean, I'll have a glass of wine at a networking dinner or a charity gala—maybe a Cabernet, something dry, because you have to hold a glass in your hand at those things, it's just expected in my circle—but that's maybe once a month, if that. And as for recreational drugs? Never. I've never touched them. I run a multimillion-dollar enterprise; I can't afford to have my mind clouded by anything like that. I need to be sharp. I need to be ten steps ahead of the board, especially now with all the whispering and the plotting. 

And medications... no, nothing new. I take a multivitamin in the morning, just a standard one, and sometimes an ibuprofen if I get a tension headache from staring at spreadsheets all day, but that's it. I don't take stimulants, I don't take sleeping pills, I don't even drink energy drinks. Just my coffee. I have my two cups of black coffee in the morning, which I've been doing since I was in my twenties, so that's certainly not new. 

I know what you're getting at, Doctor. You're wondering if maybe I'm hallucinating because I took something, or if I'm having some kind of strange reaction to a pill. I've read about that kind of thing. But I assure you, my system is completely clean. The voices I'm hearing—the CFO, the investors, coming through the glass and the powered-down phone—they aren't some chemical side effect. They're real. I just need to figure out the acoustics of how they're projecting their voices into my private office. But no, to answer your question, no drugs, no new medications, barely any alcohol. Just me, my coffee, and my work.

He was standing in the kitchen, making dinner—he usually makes this incredible roasted salmon on Sundays, it's sort of our tradition—and he just stopped and looked at me and said I've become a completely different person. And... I suppose, looking at it objectively, he's right. I mean, I barely speak to him anymore. I come home, I put my bag down, and I just sit there in the living room. I don't have the energy to ask about his day, and I certainly don't have the desire to talk about mine. 

And it's not just at home with him, it's at the office, too. Which is honestly the hardest part for me to admit, because my business is my life. Or, at least, it used to be. I used to be the person driving every single idea. I was the absolute engine of that company. If we had a new product launch or a promotional opening, I was the one working the room, calling people the very next morning, following up on every single lead, pushing my team to be better, faster, sharper. I loved it. I absolutely lived for that thrill. 

But now... I don't know. It's like someone just unplugged me from the wall. Lately, I can go into my office, shut the door, and just sit at my desk for hours. Literally hours. My assistant will print out the daily agenda and place it right in front of me, right on my desk blotter, and I will just stare at it. I won't read it. I won't action anything on it. I just stare at the bullet points until the letters don't even look like real words anymore. I barely speak to my staff at all now—I've been communicating almost entirely through very brief emails, if I communicate at all, because I just can't bring myself to actually open my mouth and have a conversation with them. 

It's the strangest, most unsettling feeling, Doctor, because I look at this company I built from nothing, this work that I used to love so much that it was practically my entire identity, and I feel almost nothing. No excitement, no pride, no urgency. Just this heavy, flat blankness. I sit there staring at the agenda, knowing intellectually that I should care, knowing I should be calling our suppliers or rallying the marketing team, but I just... don't. It's like the part of me that felt anything at all for this business has just completely evaporated.
When did you first start noticing this loss of interest and energy—did it begin around the same time as the voices three months ago, or did it start earlier or later than that?

Oh, no, no, it wasn't three months ago. Three months ago is just when the whispering and the plotting through the glass started. The... the heavy feeling, that blankness I was just telling you about? That's been building for much, much longer. 

If I really sit down and trace it back, it's been about two years and four months. I know the exact timeline because that was right when we finalized a massive company expansion. We had just acquired this boutique firm and created a brand new arts-and-commerce division. It was supposed to be the absolute crown jewel of our portfolio—this brilliant concept merging high-end artisan curation with our scalable retail logistics. It was a massive undertaking, millions of dollars on the line, and the board, of course, put me directly in charge of it. They said I was the only one with the vision to steer the ship and bridge the gap between the creatives and the corporate side. 

And at first, I thought, well, this is just fatigue. Anyone would be exhausted after a merger like that. The endless legal meetings, the zoning issues, the late-night conference calls with overseas suppliers, the sheer logistics of integrating two completely different corporate cultures... it was grueling. But then the merger finished. The arts-and-commerce division was up and running, the ribbon was cut, and... my energy never came back. 

In fact, it just started slipping away more and more. I remember sitting in the first quarterly review for that new division, looking at a chart that showed we were beating our projections by twelve percent, and I felt absolutely nothing. No thrill, no victory. Just... flat. And it's just been this slow, creeping drain ever since then. Month after month, year after year. So by the time the voices actually started three months ago, I was already practically a ghost at my own desk. It's like that expansion just slowly siphoned the life out of me over the last two and a half years, long before anyone started talking about me through the walls.
